content: Special education refers to tailored or modified instruction designed to meet the unique needs of students with specific challenges, such as learning disabilities, mental health issues, physical or developmental disabilities, or exceptional abilities (giftedness). In North America, the term special education is most commonly associated with students who have learning disabilities or mental health conditions. The provision of special education services varies significantly across countries and even within states or regions. Access to specific educational settings depends on factors such as the student’s individual needs, geographic location, family preferences, and government policies. Special educators often describe a continuum of services, where students with special needs receive varying levels of support depending on their interaction with the general school population. Special education is typically delivered through one or a combination of the following models: 1. Inclusion: In this model, students with special needs are educated alongside their typically developing peers for at least half of the school day. Full inclusion involves providing specialized services directly within the regular classroom, with service providers working with the student(s) in that setting. Partial inclusion involves students leaving the regular classroom for specific, more intensive sessions, such as speech therapy or occupational therapy. Inclusion is generally suited for students who do not require intensive support. 2. Mainstreaming: This model combines regular education classes with special education classes. Students with special needs join their typically developing peers during specific periods, depending on their skills. Mainstreaming is designed for students who need significant support and may struggle in a regular classroom environment. 3. Segregation: In this model, students with special needs are placed full-time in special education classes and do not interact with typically developing students. Segregation is intended for students who require intensive support or cannot manage even brief participation in a regular classroom. These students may attend the same school as their peers but remain in separate classrooms, or they may attend specialized schools designed to meet their needs. 4. Exclusion: Students whose disabilities prevent them from attending any school are considered excluded. These students may receive one-on-one or group instruction in settings such as hospitals, their homes, or detention facilities. Residential centers, which provide live-in schooling with medical care and various therapies, may be categorized as either segregation or exclusion. Suspended or expelled students are not considered excluded in this context. Modifications in special education can include changes to the curriculum, the use of supplementary aides or equipment, and the provision of specialized facilities to enable students to participate in the educational environment to the fullest extent possible. These supports may address academic, physical, or emotional needs and are tailored to the individual student. Support can be short-term or long-term, depending on the student’s requirements. In the United States, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) mandates that students with special needs be included in regular education activities as much as possible. In Scotland, the Additional Support Needs Act requires education authorities to meet the needs of all students in collaboration with other agencies and parents. Abbreviations for special education vary by region. In North America, terms like Special Ed, Spec Ed, or SPED are commonly used. In England and Wales, SEN (Special Educational Needs) is the standard term. In Scotland, while SEN is not official terminology, it is often used interchangeably with ASN (Additional Support Needs) due to the implementation of the Additional Support for Learning Act. Criticism of Special Education: Conducting large-scale empirical studies in special education has been challenging due to variations in service delivery models. A meta-analysis found no significant relationship between student outcomes and inclusion in special education. The qualification criteria for special education services are highly variable across educational agencies, leading to inconsistencies. At-risk students (those with educational needs not associated with a disability) are often placed in classes with students with disabilities, which critics argue may hinder the progress of students with disabilities. Disability activists criticize the segregation of special education programs from regular education, despite the push for inclusion. Inclusion practices have been criticized for not adequately addressing the diverse instructional needs of students with disabilities, potentially causing them to fall further behind their peers. Parents of typically developing children sometimes express concerns that the needs of fully included students with disabilities may divert attention and resources from the rest of the class. Eligibility criteria for special education services can be contentious, with some students being placed in programs against their wishes or denied access despite needing support. Alternative educational models, such as Sudbury schools or unschooling, propose individualized learning approaches that some proponents claim eliminate learning disabilities. Academic Resources: Journals such as the Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities, British Journal of Learning Disabilities, and British Journal of Special Education provide research and insights into the field. Other notable publications include Clinical Child Psychology and Psychiatry, Developmental Neurorehabilitation, and Disability & Society. Books like Holistic Special Education: Camphill Principles and Practice by Robin Jackson offer additional perspectives. These resources contribute to the ongoing discussion and development of best practices in special education.
